indiaMissions/india-medical-missions/tit: Medical missions: Clara Swain, Ida Scudder (Vellore), Ludhiana, Miraj
indiaMissions/india-medical-missions/sum: Medical missions grew from a handful of missionary doctors in the early nineteenth century into a vast network of hospitals, dispensaries, leprosy homes, nursing schools and medical colleges. Women doctors were decisive: Clara Swain (Bareilly, 1870), Edith Brown (Ludhiana, 1894) and Ida Scudder (Vellore, 1900) reached secluded women whom male doctors could not treat and trained the first generations of Indian women doctors and nurses. Christian Medical College Vellore and Christian Medical College Ludhiana remain among India's leading medical institutions.
indiaMissions/india-medical-missions/sto:
John Thomas, the surgeon who sailed with William Carey in 1793, was the first Protestant medical missionary in Bengal, but systematic medical mission began with the American physician John Scudder, who went to Ceylon in 1819 and moved to Madras in 1836. His descendants — more than forty Scudders served in India over four generations — became the founding dynasty of medical mission in the Arcot region. Through the nineteenth century missions attached dispensaries to mission stations, convinced that healing was both Christ-like compassion and an effective way to gain a hearing; the CMS hospital in Srinagar, founded by Robert Elmslie in 1864–65 and later run by Arthur and Ernest Neve, became famous across the northern frontier.

The seclusion of women created the strongest argument for women doctors. In 1869 the Methodist Woman's Foreign Missionary Society sent Clara Swain, a graduate of the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania, who reached Bareilly in January 1870 as the first fully qualified woman medical missionary in Asia. She began training a class of Indian girls in medicine, and the Nawab of Rampur gave land on which a women's hospital opened in 1874 — now the Clara Swain Hospital. Anna Kugler (Lutheran, Guntur, 1883), Fanny Butler (CEZMS, Kashmir and Bhagalpur, 1880s) and Elizabeth Bielby of Lucknow followed; Bielby carried a message from the Maharani of Panna to Queen Victoria in 1881, which led to the secular Countess of Dufferin's Fund (1885) for medical aid to Indian women.

In Ludhiana the English doctor Edith Brown founded the North India School of Medicine for Christian Women in 1894, training Indian women as doctors, compounders and nurses; it became the Christian Medical College Ludhiana and admitted men from 1964. In the Deccan the American Presbyterian William Wanless opened a hospital at Miraj in 1894 and trained Indian medical assistants there; the Miraj mission hospital became a major surgical centre in western India and Wanless was knighted in 1928. Leprosy work grew from the Mission to Lepers founded in 1874 by Wellesley Bailey after his experience at Ambala; mission leprosy homes at Purulia, Chandkhuri and elsewhere were for decades almost the only care available, and mission sanatoria such as the Union Mission Tuberculosis Sanatorium at Arogyavaram (1915) pioneered TB treatment.

Ida Sophia Scudder, granddaughter of John Scudder, was born at Ranipet in 1870. Visiting her parents in 1890, she was called in one night to three women dying in childbirth whose husbands refused a male doctor; all three died, and she resolved to study medicine, graduating from Cornell in 1899 in one of the first classes to admit women. She returned in 1900, opened a one-bed dispensary in Vellore and in 1902 the 40-bed Mary Taber Schell Memorial Hospital. From 1906 she ran roadside clinics by bullock cart and then motor car, started a nursing school (1909) and in 1918 opened the Missionary Medical School for Women, which received over 150 applications in its first year; the first class graduated in 1922 with notable success in the Madras government examinations. Supported by a growing union of missions in Britain and America, the school became Christian Medical College, granting Madras University degrees from 1942 and admitting men from 1947.

After independence medical missions faced the withdrawal of foreign personnel, rising costs and competition from government services. Vellore absorbed international talent such as the surgeon Paul Brand, who from 1947 developed reconstructive hand surgery for leprosy at Vellore and Karigiri (1955), and trained Indian specialists such as Mary Verghese, a paraplegic surgeon who pioneered rehabilitation medicine. Many smaller mission hospitals closed or struggled; others joined networks such as the Christian Medical Association of India (founded 1905) and the Emmanuel Hospital Association (1970), which took over mission hospitals across north India. Christian hospitals remain a significant part of Indian non-profit healthcare, especially in rural areas.

Medical mission was never only humanitarian. Waiting-room preaching, Bible readings before treatment and the expectation of a hearing in return for care were standard for much of the period, and Hindu and Muslim critics saw hospitals as instruments of conversion. Missionary medicine also disparaged Ayurvedic and Unani practitioners and traditional midwives, and leprosy asylums segregated patients in ways that later medicine regretted. Yet the hospitals, nursing schools and medical colleges trained thousands of Indian women and men at a time when few other routes into professional medicine existed for them.

indiaMissions/india-medical-missions/gro: Secluded Hindu and Muslim women who could be examined only by women doctors.
Rural villagers around mission stations, through dispensaries, travelling clinics and roadside camps.
People with leprosy, often abandoned by families, in mission leprosy homes and colonies.
Tuberculosis patients in mission sanatoria such as Arogyavaram and Madar (Ajmer).
Princely courts and elites (Rampur, Khetri, Kashmir) whose patronage aided mission hospitals.
Indian Christian women and men trained as doctors, nurses, compounders and midwives.
indiaMissions/india-medical-missions/foc: Women's and children's medicine, maternity care and midwifery.
Medical and nursing education, especially for Indian women.
Leprosy care and later reconstructive surgery and rehabilitation.
Tuberculosis, eye surgery (cataract camps) and rural community health.
Evangelism alongside treatment — preaching, Bible women and chaplaincy.
Public health in famine and epidemic years (cholera, plague, influenza 1918).
indiaMissions/india-medical-missions/str: Sending qualified women physicians to break the barrier of purdah.
Attaching a dispensary or hospital to each major mission station as a point of contact.
Training Indian assistants and nurses rather than relying solely on foreign staff.
Union institutions supported by many missions (Vellore was backed by some forty missions by mid-century; Ludhiana likewise).
Mobile clinics and medical camps reaching villages far from hospitals.
Networking through the Christian Medical Association of India and, after 1970, hospital associations that pooled resources.
indiaMissions/india-medical-missions/cha: Distrust of Western medicine and fear of conversion, especially among high-caste and Muslim families.
Shortage of qualified staff and money; many hospitals depended on a single missionary doctor.
Government regulation of medical education: Vellore and Ludhiana had to upgrade to university standards or close.
Withdrawal of foreign missionaries and funds after 1947 and tighter foreign-contribution rules (FCRA).
Competition from expanding government and private hospitals and rising costs of modern medicine.
Tension between charitable care for the poor and financial sustainability.
indiaMissions/india-medical-missions/har: Patients were often required to hear sermons or Bible readings before treatment, making care conditional on exposure to proselytism.
Missionaries frequently dismissed Ayurveda, Unani and traditional midwives as superstition, undermining local healing knowledge.
Leprosy asylums enforced segregation and separation of children from parents, and some homes encouraged or expected conversion.
Mission medicine was entangled with colonial power and princely patronage, and served as propaganda for missionary societies at home.
Some modern Christian hospitals have faced criticism for high fees and labour disputes that sit uneasily with their charitable origins.
indiaMissions/india-medical-missions/out: Christian Medical College Vellore and Christian Medical College Ludhiana became among India's most respected medical schools and hospitals.
Many of India's early women doctors and a large share of its trained nurses came from mission schools; nursing as a profession was long dominated by Christian women, especially from Kerala.
Mission leprosy work contributed to treatment and research that helped India eliminate leprosy as a public health problem (declared 2005).
A lasting network of rural Christian hospitals coordinated by the CMAI and the Emmanuel Hospital Association.
Influence on secular policy: the Dufferin Fund (1885) and later government women's medical services built on the missionary example.

indiaMissions/india-medical-missions/leg: Medical missions left the most widely admired legacy of Christianity in India: hospitals and colleges that serve patients of every religion and have trained generations of Indian doctors and nurses, many of them women. Their founders combined compassion, professional ambition and evangelistic purpose in ways that critics then and now have questioned, and the expectation that care would open doors for preaching gave real grounds for suspicion. Yet institutions like Vellore show how mission foundations could become national institutions, governed by Indians and valued well beyond the Christian community.
